newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FOCUS-Russian markets hesitate on Yeltsin health.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Russian markets hesitate on Yeltsin health.

text.p: The raging Russian equities market stopped in its tracks on Thursday after President Boris Yeltsin went to hospital with pneumonia but an early slide levelled off and other markets firmed as dealers awaited developments.
Hesitant equities traders marked down share prices before trading and major stocks opened below Wednesday's close on the Russian Trading System (RTS).
Bellwether utility Mosenergo dropped to $1.25 at 0940 GMT from $1.33 at Wednesday's close, but firmed from $1.14 in early trade.
Oil company Surgutneftegaz, which has led the market higher in the recent holiday rally, dropped to $0.558 from $0.600, but was off an early low of $0.535.

The Kremlin said the 65-year-old president, who is in Moscow's Central Clinical Hospital, had pneumonia but a normal temperature. Yeltsin returned to work only on December 23 following heart surgery on November 5.

Traders said the market could fall sharply on Yeltsin's health, the most important market factor in trade last autumn, but would not necessarily lose holiday gains which saw the RTS index jump to 227.73 on Wednesday from 189.08 on December 24.
"Moscow dealers will probably not be buying because they are too nervous," predicted Alexei Genkin, a trader at Alfa-Capital bank in Moscow.
But dealers said the market, in the middle of a bull run, was waiting for further news on Yeltsin's health.
Foreign interest in Russian private and government securities is strong with a rally widely expected in equities, despite possible corrections along the way.
The RTS broke its volume record on Wednesday when $50 million in shares changed hands, about twice what is considered a healthy day's trade.

T-bill yields are expected to fall over the year, while investors can avoid a new 15 percent profit tax on government securities likely to come into effect at the end of the month, by buying T-bills issued before then.

Robert Devane, head of fixed income at Troika-Dialog bank in Moscow, said before Yeltsin's hospitalisation was announced that the market was increasingly willing to believe official reports on the president's health.
"Unlike communist times, a president's cold does not mean he has been dead for three weeks," he said.
Deutsche Morgan Grenfell's head of research, Jim Nail, said at the same time that the health factor had less potential than last autumn, when Yeltsin underwent heart surgery.
"The importance of the Yeltsin health issue is not over yet, but I don't know anybody who has really been including the Yeltsin-dies scenario any more."

Russian Treasury bill prices firmed by up to one percent in morning trade, which dealers said reflected unsatisfied demand at a government auction on Wednesday. Dealers said the market was not unduly affected by the Yeltsin health news.
"If you look at recent history, the T-bill market has never reacted particularly to such events," said Andrei Semyonov, trader at Aljba-Alliance.
MinFin bonds also firmed after falling sharply in New York on Wednesday on news Yeltsin was back in hospital.

"New York hit MinFins late yesterday in thin trading. But today people seem confident Yeltsin is going to be all right and find these levels attractive for buying," National Reserve Bank dealer Denis Pakhomov said.
The rouble, which is strictly controlled by the central bank, was unchanged on the Moscow Interbank Currency Exchange (MICEX) at 5,595 per dollar.
